Qwen on Mac mini M4 32GB: 9B, 27B and 35B benchmarks

On a 32GB Mac mini M4, the November 1 medium-prompt runs reached 19.54 tok/s for Qwen3.5-9B 4-bit and 44.57 tok/s for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 4-bit in Rapid-MLX. The November 7 oMLX recheck generated at 34–39 tok/s and took 129 s to produce the first token from an unloaded model. Start with 9B 4-bit if memory is tight, and test both response time and memory pressure with your own prompts.

Qwen speed and memory

Swipe or scroll the tables to see all columns.

These Rapid-MLX 0.16.10 records use a 916-token prompt and 64 output tokens. Each row is an individual run. The locally served 27B build is labeled Qwen3.8-27B in the original notes. It used multi-token prediction (MTP) and reused 896 prompt tokens, so its first-token time reflects a different starting condition.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B uses a sparse mixture of experts. It can activate roughly 3B parameters per token while still needing access to the much larger set of weights. This is one reason model size alone gives an incomplete prediction of decode speed. Qwen model card

Rapid-MLX reports decimal GB (bytes divided by 1 billion). The oMLX table below reports GiB (bytes divided by 230) and measures loaded model allocation. macOS memory pressure includes other apps, cache, buffers, and swap. The 27B and 35B Rapid-MLX runs lack synchronized memory readings for a four-way comparison. For Ollama GGUF files, use the Ollama memory calculator to estimate weight and context costs separately.

How much memory does oMLX expert offload save?

In oMLX 0.7.3, lowering expert residency let the engine stream nonresident experts from the checkpoint on an external USB drive. The same 35B-A3B 4-bit weights were used in each run. Prefix caching was disabled and macOS file cache was left in place.

Warm 916-token repeat, 64 output tokens
Expert residencyLoaded modelFirst tokenGeneration
100%18.48 GiB1.96 s43.50 tok/s
75%14.37 GiB3.17 s17.01 tok/s
50%10.16 GiB5.94 s13.53 tok/s

At 75% residency, loaded model allocation dropped by about 4.1 GiB and decode fell from 43.50 to 17.01 tok/s. At 50%, the allocation dropped by about 8.3 GiB and decode fell to 13.53 tok/s. These are changes in the loaded model metric. Memory pressure and response time can change with context size, the system's file cache, and the storage device. This test does not isolate cold drive reads or cover a 90% setting. oMLX expert offload implementation

Why the first token can take minutes

The first token includes time spent loading the model if it is unloaded, plus scheduling and prompt processing. Generation speed measures output after streaming has begun. In one Rapid-MLX run the first short request took 59.93 s to start, while a later medium request took 3.52 s. Both generated at about 44.6 tok/s.

Separate oMLX prefix-cache observations at full residency
RequestInput / cached tokensFirst token
First medium916 / 02.084 s
Repeat medium916 / 9090.119 s
Follow-up994 / 9090.559 s
Repeat short32 / 258.944 s

The repeated short prompt hit the cache and still took 8.944 s to start. The test did not isolate the reason. Record the first and repeated request separately, along with prompt length and cached tokens. A large context window can cost more to process even if short prompts start quickly.

November 7 recheck

The same Mac mini with macOS build 25E253 ran oMLX 0.7.3 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B full resident, with MTP off and no model loaded at the start. Each request produced 64 tokens. Two serial rounds finished. The third ended at a health check with a reset connection.

oMLX 35B-A3B, two serial rounds
RequestInput / cached tokensFirst tokenGeneration
First short, model unloaded32 / 0129.12 s33.98 tok/s
First medium, model loaded916 / 03.61 s36.93 tok/s
Repeat short32 / 250.58 s34.65 tok/s
Repeat medium916 / 9090.17 s39.04 tok/s

Loaded model allocation was 19.08 GiB after both rounds. The first 129.12 s measurement includes loading and inference. The 0.17 s repeat reused 909 of 916 tokens. It captures a single repeat. November 7 per-request data

Check which Qwen model fits your Mac

  1. In Activity Monitor, open Memory and note Memory Pressure and Swap Used with your normal apps running. Load one model at a time, then check the readings again during a representative request. Apple Activity Monitor guide
  2. Start with Qwen3.5-9B 4-bit when headroom is limited. If you want the faster sustained generation measured here, try 35B-A3B 4-bit at full residency and observe the difference in pressure. When swap keeps growing under the same work, try a smaller model or shorter context and repeat. If you use expert offload to keep 35B, retest first-token time and generation.
  3. Run your actual format, accuracy, and tool tests before choosing. In a small November 1 check with thinking off, both 9B builds passed five of seven checks and failed two arithmetic or reasoning prompts. The 35B build missed those two prompts too. The samples provide no general quality ranking.

Our 32GB host kept 35B-A3B in oMLX at full residency for this deployment. Treat 16GB, 24GB, different M-series chips, and long context as separate setups. Start with the local LLM setup guide if you still need a running endpoint.

Test conditions and limits

Hardware was one base Mac mini M4 with 32GB unified memory. The November 1 records came from engineering runs in Rapid-MLX 0.16.10 and oMLX 0.7.3. Single-concurrency streaming used temperature 0, thinking off, and up to 64 completion tokens. The service reported approximately 32 and 916 input tokens for the two prompts. OS builds were not consistently recorded for that set. The 27B warm sample predates the additional November 1 checks.

Decode speed is (output tokens − 1) / (total seconds − first-token seconds). The script records the first streamed content or reasoning chunk. The calculation covers steady output, so it excludes first-token wait. No matched long-context, image, power, multi-user, p95, or stability tests were run.

Download the data and benchmark your own setup

November 1 results · November 7 recheck · Python streaming benchmark

Start an OpenAI-compatible server on loopback, download the script, and replace the port or server model ID below. For a password-protected endpoint, pass its key in LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY.

python3 benchmark-qwen-stream.py \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \
  --model YOUR_MODEL_ID

Keep the model, engine version, quantization, prompt, residency, cache settings, and concurrency with your results. For Ollama, the Ollama timing guide uses native API durations for its separate input and output rates.
